newsitem.title: INDIA: India finds decision on oil price rises slippery.
newsitem.headline: India finds decision on oil price rises slippery.

text.p: Whatever Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda says, a stiff rise in state controlled petroleum prices is needed soon as domestic oil firms are creaking under the strain of India's subsidy regime, analysts said on Tuesday.
World oil prices near six-year highs have created a budget migraine for India, testing oil companies' pain threshold.
Deve Gowda on Monday appeared to rule out any imminent rise in domestic product prices after newspapers reported the Petroleum Ministry favoured a 20 percent rise.
"The whole thing should have happened three to four months ago. Now the sooner it happens the better, as the oil pool deficit is growing," said one analyst, who requested anonymity.
The oil pool deficit account is effectively the amount the government owes India's oil companies for selling petroleum products to Indian consumers way below world prices.
Under the administered pricing mechanism, India's oil companies carry the burden on their cash flows for the oil pool deficit while they wait for the state to pay them back.
But the fragile United Front coalition led by Deve Gowda is tip-toeing around the oil price minefield while a deepening oil pool saps companies' strength.

Last July, after just one month in office, the government raised petroleum prices sharply, but in the past few months the case for another rise has become more acute while goodwill towards Deve Gowda's coalition has sagged.
"Political considerations are not allowing them to increase petroleum product prices," said Sanjeev Patni, an oil analyst with brokers W.I. Carr.
Also, inflation will shoot up 2.5 to 3.0 percentage points, pushing the annual rate into double digits, if the product prices are raised 20 percent, Patni said.
"As of now the United Front government has no intention of taking such a step (raising oil prices)," the United News of India news agency quoted Deve Gowda as saying on Monday.
The prime minister might be more ready to act once Punjab state elections, set for February 6, were over, analysts said.
"I imagine it would probably happen in the second week of February," Dr R.K. Pachauri, director of Tata Energy Research Institute, said.
He reckoned the government would want to keep the oil price issue out of the 1997/98 (April-March) budget debate, which is expected to open in late February.
The oil pool deficit is seen reaching 160 to 200 billion rupees ($4.5 billion to $5.6 billion) in the 1996/97 financial year.
The companies can cover the money they are owed from the oil pool by borrowing, but that is eroding their creditworthiness.
The unnamed analyst said the oil pool deficit was on course to hit 160 billion rupees by March this year.
He said it meant Indian Oil Corp would be owed between 100 billion and 110 billion rupees from the oil pool. Oil and Natural Gas Corp would be owed around 30 billion rupees.
Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd and Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd would be owed between 10 billion and 12 billion rupees apiece, he said.
Prices for kerosene, which provides the fuel oil and lights up rural and semi-urban India, are subsidised by almost 80 percent, Tata Energy Research estimated.
Diesel, which runs the trucks and tractors, gets a subsidy of around 65 percent.
Liquefied petroleum gas is subsidised by nearly 45 percent, and naphtha and fuel oil are subsidised by up to 22 percent.
The subsidy on kerosene accounts for around 30 percent of the oil pool and is the most touchy issue for voters and the hardest for the government to adjust. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
